# Metis — Model Validation & Comparison Report

**Generated by:** `backend/training/validate_models.py`
**Data:** Real NHANES August 2021–August 2023, 5,695 participants, 15.2% positive class (diabetes, diagnosed or lab-confirmed)
**Method:** 7 model families trained on the identical train/test split (80/20, stratified, `random_state=42`) and identical feature set as production. See that script's docstring for exactly how class imbalance and missing values were handled consistently across all 7.

## Why this study exists

The production model (XGBoost with monotonicity constraints) was chosen for two specific reasons documented in `train_model.py`: it supports **monotonicity constraints** (so the What-If simulator's levers can't move in a causally backwards direction — see the earlier `sugar_g`/`drinks_per_day` confound writeup) and it **natively handles missing data** (roughly half the fasting-subsample labs are legitimately absent, not bad data). This study checks whether that choice actually holds up against alternatives, rather than taking it on faith.

## Results

| Model | ROC-AUC | PR-AUC | Accuracy | Precision | Recall | F1 | Brier (↓ better) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic Regression | 0.869 | 0.554 | 0.785 | 0.397 | 0.798 | 0.530 | 0.150 |
| Random Forest | 0.863 | 0.505 | 0.831 | 0.457 | 0.618 | 0.526 | 0.118 |
| Gradient Boosting | 0.876 | 0.603 | 0.811 | 0.431 | 0.763 | 0.551 | 0.127 |
| HistGradientBoosting | **0.886** | **0.641** | 0.842 | 0.486 | 0.694 | 0.571 | 0.107 |
| HistGB (monotonic) | 0.856 | 0.516 | 0.805 | 0.419 | 0.728 | 0.532 | 0.135 |
| SVM | 0.855 | 0.513 | 0.856 | 0.567 | 0.220 | 0.317 | **0.098** |
| **XGBoost (production)** | 0.870 | 0.536 | 0.809 | 0.429 | 0.786 | 0.555 | 0.137 |

Full precision in `validation_results/metrics_comparison.csv`.

## What this validates

**1. The risk signal is real, not an artifact of one algorithm.** All 7 models — spanning linear, kernel, bagged-tree, and boosted-tree families — land in a tight 0.855–0.886 ROC-AUC band. If XGBoost's 0.870 only looked good in isolation, that would be a red flag; instead every reasonable model family finds essentially the same amount of signal in the same features.

**2. Convergent feature importance across model families.** `age`, `waist_height_ratio`, `homa_ir`, `total_cholesterol`, and `liver_fat_cap` rank at or near the top for Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, *and* (via coefficient magnitude) Logistic Regression — four structurally different ways of finding importance, agreeing on the same handful of drivers. That's independent evidence the SHAP explanations shown in the app reflect genuine signal rather than an XGBoost-specific quirk.

**3. Unconstrained HistGradientBoosting is the best raw discriminator (0.886 AUC) — but that's not the full picture.** This is the honest, slightly uncomfortable finding: if the only goal were maximizing ROC-AUC, HistGB would win. It was tested specifically because it's a legitimate, modern alternative with the same missing-data handling XGBoost was chosen for.

**4. Once held to the same monotonicity constraint, XGBoost wins.** Re-running HistGB with the *identical* monotonicity constraints used in production (`monotonic_cst`, sklearn ≥1.4) drops it to 0.856 AUC — below production XGBoost's constrained 0.870. In other words, XGBoost's monotonicity implementation extracts more signal *while* guaranteeing causal sanity than sklearn's does on this dataset. **This is the central validation result: the production choice isn't just defensible, it's measurably better than the closest alternative once both are held to the same real-world requirement (a simulator lever can't ever move risk the wrong direction).**

**5. SVM is a cautionary tale, visible at a glance in the confusion-matrix grid.** It has the *best* accuracy (0.856) and Brier score (0.098) but catches only 38 of 173 actual diabetes cases in the test set (recall 0.220) — it's achieving "accuracy" mostly by predicting the majority class. This is exactly the kind of failure a single headline metric (accuracy, or even Brier score) can hide, and exactly why this study reports 7 metrics and 6 visualizations rather than one number.

## Reproducing this study

```bash
cd backend/training
pip install -r requirements-validation.txt
python3 validate_models.py
```

Takes under a minute on the full 5,695-row dataset. Re-run any time the underlying data or feature set changes to re-check whether the production model choice still holds.

## Limitations of this study itself

- Single train/test split, not cross-validated — a k-fold study would give tighter confidence intervals on these metrics, at the cost of losing the "identical held-out test set for every model" framing that makes the head-to-head comparison clean.
- SVM and Logistic Regression were evaluated on median-imputed, standardized features (necessary — they can't handle missing values or unscaled inputs), while XGBoost/HistGB saw the raw data with true missingness. That's a deliberate, documented choice (see the script's docstring) reflecting how each model would actually be used, not an oversight — but it does mean the comparison isn't perfectly apples-to-apples for those two.
- No hyperparameter tuning was performed for any of the 7 — all use reasonable defaults or the production model's already-tuned config. A tuned HistGB (monotonic) might close some or all of the gap with XGBoost; this study answers "does the production choice hold up against reasonable alternatives," not "is XGBoost provably optimal."
